Now let us examine the conversation line by line.
'On your feet!' Senya replies with a single verb form meaning 'stood still' — in Russian, the verb ending alone carries the subject and tense.
'He didn't like your salad.' The verb for 'was liked' is in the masculine past tense, marked by the '-l' ending. Then Senya responds.
'He didn't try it.' Senya delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'tried'.
'Actually, he has.' Fedya expresses this naturally by combining the word for 'actually' with 'tried'.
'There was a belt in my salad.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be', connecting 'at' directly with 'belt'.
'We just had a bet.' Here Senya anchors the line on the word meaning 'just' and builds the thought around 'argued'.
'To see if I'd eat a belt?' the guest turns a statement into a question purely through rising intonation on the word meaning 'belt', followed by 'eat'.
'It wasn't me.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'this' directly with 'not', combining 'this' with 'not' and 'I'.
'You're eating this.' the guest chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'gobble' for the ongoing action, followed by 'will'.
Пока всё не съешь, не уйдёшь.
'You're not leaving until you eat it all.' Here the guest anchors the line on the word meaning 'bye' and builds the thought around 'eat' and 'you'll leave'.
'Could I have some bread?' Russian leaves out 'am', 'is', or 'are' in the present tense, linking 'may' straight to 'bread'.
'Here you go.' the guest delivers a punchy conversational reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'for'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
